3:12, every Thursday. Mara found the book in the bread rack. Same one every time: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, library stamp from a town forty miles away. She'd set it on the flour bin, wipe butter off the cover. She'd mean to take it back after her shift. By noon, errands and the heat and sleep would swallow that thought. Next Thursday it'd be there again, tucked in between the cooling rye loaves.

Tonight the bakery hummed. Proofing cabinet, old radio static, rain pressing silver lines down the front window. Mara lifted the book with both hands, kind of like it might be warm. A folded receipt marked the chapter on herons. She opened it.

In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.

She turned to page 47. Grey heron in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint. Under the picture in pencil: THURSDAY, 3:30?

The clock over the mixer clicked once.

Mara brushed flour off her apron, unlocked the front door, turned on the little OPEN sign.

This is a magical, awe-inspiring show. Its story of lost love is the backbone. The protagonist gets love right at the start, and then in an abrupt way loses it. And then the plot twists and turns in ways I didn't expect. The lighting, the water imagery, the music, the visual design, it all comes together really well, which is why there are these really, really breathtaking moments. So the actors, the dancers, they're joined by the synchronized swimmers, the acrobats, and the precision is insane. They do these wild flips, dramatic dives into the water, their synchronized swim routines, they hold their breath for so many seconds and it's just stunning. There is a lot of drama, but it also has these genuinely funny moments, and it balances out. I was totally swept up by it, and the whole production is so imaginative, so grand, but surprisingly moving. If you get the chance, go. I think it is an absolute must-see.

I really felt like magic, like awe. Lost love story, the man falls in love right at the beginning and then loses it, and it goes on and on. The lights, the water, the music, the visual design, all fit together and made things beautiful. Breathtaking moments. On stage we had actors, dancers, swimmers, acrobats, and everything very very precise, flips, dives, breathing holds. Swimmers holding their breath for many seconds, very impressive. Dramatic emotional drama and some pretty funny moments too. Just very moving really, and very imaginative and grand. If you can see it, do, it's a must see.

Its just a rain gauge for measuring rainfall by catching rain through a funnel and guiding it down into a cylindrical measuring tube.
To make it easier to read it is intentionally much wider than the tube, so any slight amount of rain is magnified and can be measured accurately.
If the mouth of the funnel is 10x the size of the measuring tube, an inch of rain will fill the tube 10 inches deep, making it possible to measure hundredths of an inch of rain.
Its subject to error though.
Water evaporates easily in warm weather or windy weather.
And wind can also throw off the measurement, strong gusts can actually throw raindrops past the mouth of the instrument, meaning it would show less rainfall than is actually occurring.

a rain gauge works by funneling precipitation into a small measuring tube. its top opening is made wider than the tube on purpose. if the mouth has say ten times the area of the inner tube, a single inch of rain fills the tube to ten inches. its an amplifier, lets you read a hundredth of an inch really precisely. not always accurate though. evaporation is a big one, the water can dry out of the tube before you measure it, in warm or windy conditions. wind causes issues too with turbulence up above the mouth, where it knocks rain off to one side. that can cause a huge error on an actual gauge.

You use a simple rain gauge to measure rain so you catch the precipitation in a funnel and send it into a cylindrical tube. The gauge is set up so that the collection opening is much bigger than the inner tube. That difference functions as an amplifier. Like, if the opening is ten times the area of the measuring tube, an inch of rain will fill the tube ten inches high. This magnification lets observers read small amounts, like hundredths of an inch, accurately. Its not perfect. A big source of errors is evaporation, water quickly evaporates before you even see it, in warm and windy conditions. Another major source of error is wind exposure. It's a common problem. The wind makes a lot of turbulence around the mouth and pushes the raindrops over the opening and the gauge will under-estimate the rainfall.

It's Thursday 3:17 am. The ovens just humming away low and steady, air smells like yeast and burnt sugar. Elias wipes flour off his forearms. Walks over to the front counter, the worn paperback is on the glass display case same as it has been for six weeks. *The Shadow of the Wind*. He picks it up, gets the familiar weight, pages dog-eared. Normally hes just put it in the return bin by the register, assumes a confused customer mistaken the drop-box for a library return bin. But tonight it feels different, book is slightly warmer than the cool shop air. He opens it to the bookmarked page. This folded square of lined notebook paper falls out and lands on the counter. Hesitates, unfolds it. Jagged, hurried writing. It says *I know you're reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything.* His heart slams on his ribs, sudden sharp rhythm, and you just have this hum of mixers. Looks around, shop is empty, shadows stretch long on the tiles. No one there. Looks at the note then at the book. Turns to page 204 with trembling fingers. The text blurs before his eyes. He closes it, presses it flat on the counter, and reaches for his pen.

There was a worn paperback on the front counter on the glass display case. The Shadow of the Wind. He picked it up. Dog-eared pages. It had been there 6 weeks. Normally he'd just pop it in the return bin, assume it's a confused customer who thought the bakery late night drop slot was a library return, but tonight it was a bit warmer than the cool shop air. He opened it to the bookmarked page. A folded square of lined paper slipped out, fluttered to the counter. He hesitated, then opened it. Jagged handwriting, hurried. It said, "I know you're reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything." His heart hammered hard. Sharp rhythm against the quiet hum of the mixers. He looked around the empty shop, shadows long across the tiled floor. No one was there. Looked back at the note. Then back at the book. With trembling fingers turned to page 204. The text blurred before his eyes. He closed it, pressed it flat against the counter, and reached for his pen.

The ovens just went on humming low and steady in the shop, air thick with yeast and burnt sugar. Elias wiped flour off his arms, glanced at the clock, 3:17 AM, Thursday. He walked up to the front counter. There was a book sitting on the glass display case, this worn paperback called *The Shadow of the Wind*. Had been there six weeks now, just sitting. Normally he would grab it and put it in the return bin behind the register, assume a mixed up customer dropped it there by mistake. But tonight it felt different. The book was warm, slightly warmer than the cold air of the shop. He opened it to a marked page, and this folded square of lined notebook paper slipped out and landed on the counter. Elias stopped for a second then opened it up. Writing was jagged and hurried. *I know you’re reading it. Keep going. Page 204 changes everything.* His heart went crazy, banging on his ribs, a sharp odd beat cutting through the quiet mixer noise. He looked around the shop. Empty. Shadows long on the tiles. Nobody there. He looked at the note, looked at the book. Hands shaking a bit, went to page 204. Words got blurry in front of his face. He closed the book, slammed it flat on the counter, and went to get his pen.

I've an orders df with 120,000 rows and a customers df with 9,000. I wanted to attach customer info to orders on customer_id. So I did a left merge.

orders is 120000 x 8 and customers is 9000 x 5, then merged comes out at 127845 x 12. Expected 120000 and each order to map to 1 customer. But the duplicates exist. For example if I filter on order_id 12345, I get the same rows: 12345 / 9876 / 2024-01-10 / Alice Smith twice. Both dfs have the same customer_id column and dtypes look right, int64 on both.
I checked nunique: orders customer_id nunique 9000 and customers customer_id nunique 8750. So in the customers table, customer_id isn't unique. The duplicates come from a many to one relationship. It's 250 customer_ids in the customers table are repeated, and the customer_id column needs to have only unique values to avoid the cartesian product.

i have an orders df around 120k rows and customers around 9k rows. i need to add customer info to the orders using customer_id.

```
orders.shape  (120000, 8)
customers.shape  (9000, 5)
merged = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")
merged.shape (127845, 12)
```

was expecting 120k rows since each order should map to one customer max. but the merge adds extra rows and i'm seeing the same order repeat.

so if i filter merged df by order_id 12345, i get 2 rows with identical customer id 9876, same date 2024-01-10, customer Alice Smith.

i went and checked unique customer id counts:
orders: 9000 unique, customers: 8750 unique.

customer id exists on both frames and the data types match - both int64.

my question is, how do i figure out why the duplicates appear on merge, and how do i confirm that each order only links to one customer?

I woke at 3:17. The bakery is all yeast smell and quiet. Marisol put the loaves in the oven and saw the book again, The Borrowers in the wicker basket by the back door. Every Thursday for six weeks somebody has put it back here and not the library two blocks over. No name, no card, just the book, faintly smells like rain and woodsmoke. This time a folded note slipped between pages 84 and 85. She put her floury hands on the counter for a second then opened it: i cant make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing its warm. Looked at the basket and the cinnamon rolls out on the rack still hot. She picked the one with the most icing, wrapped it in wax paper, put the note back in the book and left them both by the door. Then she flipped the sign to OPEN and got to the coffee.

It was 3:17am at the bakery, all yeast and quiet. Marisol put her first loaves in the oven and spotted the worn copy of The Borrowers in the wicker basket by the back door again. For six weeks every Thursday, someone's been leaving it there instead of the library two blocks over. No name on it, no card. Just the book, smells faintly like rain and woodsmoke.

Tonight she found a note folded between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. I can't make it to the library before closing, please keep it another week, it says. I like knowing it's warm. She stared at the basket, then the tray of cinnamon rolls on the cooling rack. Picked the one with the most icing. Wrapped it in wax paper, tucked the note back into the book, put both by the door. Flipped the sign to open and started the coffee.

At 3:17 am the bakery was this hush with all the yeast in the air. Marisol was sliding the first loaves into the oven. She saw that worn paperback, The Borrowers. It is always in the wicker basket by the back door, every Thursday for six weeks now instead of the library two blocks over. No name on it. No card, just the book itself, and it smells faintly of rain and woodsmoke.

Tonight, there was a folded note tucked between pages 84 and 85. She wiped her floury hands and opened it. The note read, I can’t make it to the library before closing. Please keep it another week. I like knowing it’s warm.

Marisol looked at the basket, then to the cinnamon rolls cooling on the rack. She chose the one with the most icing. Wrapped it in wax paper. Then she tucked the note back into the book. Set both by the door. And flipped the sign to OPEN, and started the coffee.
